clinical_record:
A man in his 60s presented with a 3-month history of intertrigo involving his groin that he had been treating with a combination of clotrimazole cream, 1%, and hydrocortisone cream, 1%. The condition improved, but he then developed bright red, burning and painful nodules around his scrotum. Medical history included prostate cancer, hypertension, anxiety disorder, hyperlipidemia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and diverticulosis. Current medications included omeprazole, alprazolam, amlodipine besylate, atenolol, simvastatin, and valsartan.

Two symmetrical solitary erythematous nodules were present in the right and left inguinal folds adjacent to the scrotum.

- Histopathological examination:     - Epidermal ulceration overlying a diffuse dermal proliferation composed of sheets of histiocytes with eosinophilic granular cytoplasm    - Intracytoplasmic Michaelis-Gutmann bodies present as basophilic, somewhat laminated intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies measuring 5-8 μm in diameter    - Bodies highlighted with iron (Prussian blue) and calcium (Von Kossa) stains    - Background population of many plasma cells and few neutrophils noted  - Tissue Culture:    - Fungus culture: Negative    - Atypical mycobacteria culture: Negative      - Bacterial culture: Positive for E. coli  - Images:    Image 1 Title: Clinical image of right inguinal fold    Image 1 Description: Well-demarcated erythematous solitary papule in the right inguinal fold    Image 2 Title: Excisional biopsy pathologic analysis    Image 2 Description: Ulcerated nodule with sheeted dermal proliferation and histiocytes with pink granular cytoplasm containing laminated slightly basophilic inclusions (Michaelis-Gutmann bodies) with background plasma cells and neutrophils    Image 3 Title: Special stain results    Image 3 Description: Prussian blue and Von Kossa stains highlighting Michaelis-Gutmann bodies

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.reason: This candidate is a broader term for malakoplakia without specifying the cutaneous location, which is clearly indicated in the clinical record.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: Intracytoplasmic Michaelis-Gutmann bodies
reviewer_b.reason: Malakoplakia is the same disease entity as the reference; the cutaneous location is implied by the clinical context and histopathology.

clinical_record:
A 55-year-old white woman with a history of diverticulosis and colonic polyps presented with new-onset flulike symptoms followed by low-grade fever, facial crusted plaques, and 4 weeks of bloody and watery diarrhea. Her facial lesions initially presented as ill-defined pink patches over her cheeks and red papules on her forehead. Over the next 4 days, the lesions spread to her chest, abdomen, back, and left buttock, and a single papule appeared on the right lower extremity. Her low-grade fevers and diarrhea persisted throughout this 4-day period.

In the emergency department, she was febrile and tachycardic. Physical findings included:- 6 × 7-cm well-demarcated vegetative crusted plaques on the bilateral cheeks- Several discrete, round, 1- to 2-cm crusted plaques on the temple- Discrete pustules, vesicles, and umbilicated papules on cheeks and temple- Lesions on chest, abdomen, back, and left buttock- Painful subcutaneous nodules over lower extremities- Polyarthralgia

Laboratory Tests:- Mild leukocytosis with normal differential- Mildly elevated transaminase and alkaline phosphatase levels- Negative wound culture- Blood cultures showed no growth- Negative PCR for herpes simplex virus- Negative direct fluorescent antibody assay for varicella-zoster virusPathology:- Forehead lesion biopsy: Intradermal neutrophilic inflammation with ulceration and intracorneal neutrophils. Special stains negative for microorganisms- Right thigh biopsy: Septal panniculitis with Miescher radial granulomas- Colonoscopy: Moderate inflammation, edema, erosions, and pseudopolyps in the sigmoid colonImages:Image 1 Title: Clinical Appearance of Facial Neutrophilic DermatosisImage 1 Description: A, A 6 × 7-cm, well-demarcated, vegetative crusted plaque on the left cheek and a discrete, round, 1- to 2-cm crusted plaque on the foreheadImage 2 Title: Histopathological Findings of Facial Neutrophilic DermatosisImage 2 Description: Shave biopsy specimen from forehead lesion showing diffuse intradermal neutrophilic infiltrate with central ulceration

clinical_record:
A patient in their 60s presented to the emergency department with approximately 20 minutes of acute, severe precordial chest pain radiating to their left arm at night, accompanied by dyspnea, dizziness, and sweating. The patient's medical history was notable for hypertension, cerebral infarction, diabetes, and nicotine addiction.

Vital signs showed blood pressure of 188/101 mm Hg, heart rate at 84 beats/min, and respiratory rate at 20 breaths/min.

- Laboratory tests:
  - Serum cardiac troponin I level: <0.05 ng/mL (normal range, <0.16 ng/mL)
  - Potassium level: 4.1 mEq/L (normal range, 3.5-5.3 mEq/L)

- ECG findings:
  Image A Title: Initial ECG
  Image A Description: ECG showed a sinus rhythm at a rate of 85 beats/min with the presence of broad-based, asymmetrical, tall upright T waves in precordial leads V2 through V5

  Image B Title: Post-procedural ECG
  Image B Description: Sinus rhythm at 65 beats/min with normalization of the T-wave morphology in leads V2 through V5

- Coronary angiography:
  Finding: Subtotal occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: Subtotal occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery
reviewer_a.reason: The patient presents with acute chest pain, ECG changes (tall T waves in V2-V5), and coronary angiography showing subtotal occlusion of the LAD, all consistent with acute myocardial infarction. The normal troponin is unusual but can occur early in the presentation.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: Subtotal occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery
reviewer_b.reason: Acute MI is the correct family but lacks the window-period specificity.

clinical_record:
A woman in her 30s with a history of right breast cancer, stage IIIa (cT2N2M0). She underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by right modified radical mastectomy and postoperative radiotherapy. After radiotherapy, she noticed a pruritic erythema lesion with multiple nodules over the operation site of the right breast. The lesion did not respond to initial topical treatments. Three months later (1 year after initial cancer diagnosis), she presented to dermatology for evaluation of skin erythema over her right breast.

A well-demarcated, warm, erythematous plaque, 15 × 12 cm, was seen over the right side of the anterior chest wall around her operation scar. Scattered within the erythema were multiple palpable small nodules.

- Immunohistochemistry:   Negative for estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)- Skin Biopsy:  Multiple emboli of carcinoma cells in dermal and subcutaneous lymphatic vessels- Images:  Image Title: Postmastectomy Clinical Images Before and After Treatment  Image Description A: Right mastectomy scar with a large well-defined area of erythema and multiple, scattered small nodules  Image Description B: Nearly complete remission of skin lesions after treatment

reviewer_a.reason: This candidate correctly identifies the specific type of cutaneous metastasis but omits the origin from triple-negative breast cancer.

A 67-year-old female presented with three-year history of worsening dysarthria and dysphagia, choking episodes provoked when lying supine, a one-year history of constant pain at right occipital and cervical paraspinal areas and a 20-pound weight loss. She had lingual and palatal dysarthria, and slow, but symmetric palate elevation. The rest of her neurological exam, including muscle and facial strength and reflexes, was unremarkable.

clinical_record:
A 67-year-old male with a past medical history of hypertension and coronary artery disease presented with episodes of prominent dizziness, vertigo, intermittent left arm shaking, and bouts of dull response that occurred while playing Mah-Jong with his friends. During the attacks, he was partially aware of what was happening but unable to think. Each episode lasted about 5 minutes. The attacks recurred more than 10 times a day. He had no prior history of seizures.

Blood pressure was 200/110 mmHg at triage. Neurological examination was unremarkable except for the presence of a dull response during the events. There were no focal brainstem signs, left-right disorientation, dyslexia, dysgraphia, or finger agnosia. No extraocular movement deviation, trismus, or incontinence was observed.

- Laboratory tests: Basic laboratory data were within normal limits.- Imaging studies:  Brain MRI revealed non-specific white matter changes with no signal alterations in the posterior circulation or brainstem.  - EEG findings:  Title: Right hemispheric rhythmic activities  Description: Rhythmic epileptiform discharges originating from the right frontal area with ipsilateral hemispheric spreading and relatively limited homologous contralateral involvement. Activities appeared in a quasi-periodic fashion at intervals of about one second, during which the patient presented significant dizziness, vertigo and dull response.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: Rhythmic epileptiform discharges originating from the right frontal area with ipsilateral hemispheric spreading and relatively limited homologous contralateral involvement.
reviewer_a.reason: The patient's symptoms (dizziness, vertigo, dull response, partial awareness, no convulsive movements) combined with EEG showing rhythmic epileptiform discharges originating from the right frontal area with hemispheric spreading are characteristic of complex partial seizures (now focal impaired awareness seizures).

reviewer_b.decisive_span: Rhythmic epileptiform discharges originating from the right frontal area
reviewer_b.reason: Complex partial seizure is a specific seizure type that fits the focal epileptiform activity and altered awareness, but the reference is broader and non-convulsive nature is not confirmed.

A woman in her 40s presented with blurred vision in the right eye. She was undergoing treatment with systemic steroids, durvalumab (a PD-L1 inhibitor), and bevacizumab. Ten days after initial presentation, the patient developed sudden vision loss in the right eye.

clinical_record:
An obese man in his mid-30s with no prior systemic or ocular disorders presented to a local emergency department after waking with vision loss in his right eye. The night prior, he had been drinking alcohol heavily and took 2 buprenorphine hydrochloride/naloxone hydrochloride pills. He denied any trauma. He also experienced pain, numbness, and erythematous induration of his right eyelids and forearm that increased throughout the day.

Visual acuity: No light perception in right eye (OD) and 20/20 in left eye (OS). Right eye showed tense eyelid edema, chemosis, corneal haze, and restricted motility in all fields of gaze. Right pupil was mid-dilated with a relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure was 37 mm Hg OD and 21 mm Hg OS. Ophthalmoscopic examination revealed tortuous vessels, serous retinal detachment sparing the inferior periphery, and macular whitening. Left eye examination was normal.

- Laboratory Tests:
Creatinine level: 2.2 mg/dL
Creatine kinase level: 29,320 U/L

3. Fluorescein Angiography:
Image Title: Fluorescein Angiography of the Right Eye

She had lipolymphedema of the lower legs attributed to functional venous insufficiency with insufficient venous pump activity, and had been wearing compression stockings for years. Family history revealed similar conditions in the patient's father and aunt, with the father having died of an intracranial hemorrhage in his early 70s.

Multiple bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules on the lower legs. Lipolymphedema of the lower legs was present. Right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia were noted.

A 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy was transferred at 31 weeks 5 days’ gestation. • Twin 2: estimated fetal weight 1128 g (<5th centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and MCA-PSV 50.9 cm/s (1.3 MoM).  
Placental imaging showed a normal-appearing placenta for twin 1 and a thickened, echogenic placenta for twin 2. These findings prompted suspicion for twin anemia-polycythemia sequence and an emergency cesarean section at 32 + 2 weeks.

A 44-year-old woman from Veracruz, Mexico, of low socioeconomic status, with systemic lupus erythematosus since 2003 (cutaneous, joint, and renal involvement), presented with a one-week history of progressive headache, phonophobia, high-grade fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. One month earlier, she had been treated for SLE-associated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with plasmapheresis, cyclophosphamide, and prednisone at 1 mg/kg per day.

On admission she had systemic inflammatory response syndrome and nuchal rigidity but no focal neurologic deficits or clinical signs of lupus activity. Lumbar puncture revealed a pH of 7.35, glucose 45 mg/dL (serum glucose 130 mg/dL), protein 329 mg/dL, 42 white cells/mm3 (95% neutrophils), and 2 red cells/mm3. Cerebrospinal fluid culture grew Enterococcus gallinarum, and she was treated with intravenous ampicillin, with improvement in her neurologic symptoms.

On hospital day 3, she developed hemoptysis, bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiograph, a drop in hemoglobin concentration, and acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation and ICU admission. Cultures were obtained, and she was started on methylprednisolone boluses and broad-spectrum antibiotics. The initial clinical diagnosis was diffuse alveolar hemorrhage caused by SLE activity without sufficient clinical criteria of nosocomial pneumonia.

On hospital day 4, she developed a purpuric skin rash, and a skin biopsy was performed.

clinical_record:
A 34-year-old North African woman with no significant past medical history was referred for management of obstructive jaundice. Two months earlier, she had undergone laparotomy and resection of the protruding dome of a segment I hepatic cyst thought to be a hydatid cyst compressing the biliary convergence. She now presented with fever to 38.5 °C, mucocutaneous jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. On examination, she was febrile and icteric; there was no abdominal tenderness, hepatomegaly, or palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed moderate hepatocellular enzyme elevations and cholestasis. Hydatid serology and serum carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen levels were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a cystic lesion in segment I with parietal and septal enhancement and rupture into the biliary convergence. MRI demonstrated a multiloculated lesion that was hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, communicating with the biliary bifurcation, with dilatation of intrahepatic ducts (predominantly left) and of the common bile duct containing heterogeneous signal material. At laparotomy via a subcostal incision, the liver appeared micronodular; on opening the common bile duct, mucinous fluid and membranes were extracted, raising questions about the presumed diagnosis.

reviewer_a.reason: The clinical presentation, imaging, and mucinous fluid are highly suggestive of a biliary mucinous cystic neoplasm. 'Cystadenoma' implies benign, which cannot be definitively confirmed without histology, but it is a strong possibility.

• Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)

Her past medical history was notable for excision of a dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans in the left inguinal–suprapubic region in 1998, with four local recurrences (2000, 2001, 2008, and 2009) treated surgically; she also received external radiotherapy (66 Gy) after the last excision.

On examination, there was a large, firm, mildly tender mass on the right side of the neck without fixation; the Pemberton sign was positive. Laboratory studies showed:
• TSH 0.363 mIU/L (0.32–5.0)  
• Free T4 14.6 pmol/L (9.0–19.0)  
• Anti-thyroglobulin antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)  
• Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)  
• Intact PTH 6 pmol/L (1.48–8.43)

Ultrasound of the thyroid revealed a right lobe volume of 50 mL and left lobe 7.3 mL; the entire right lobe was replaced by a hypo- to anechoic mass measuring approximately 6 × 4 × 6 cm, displacing the trachea 1 cm to the left, with no pathological lymphadenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the right lobe yielded a hemorrhagic background with isolated clusters of pleomorphic round and oval nuclei; it was classified as category IV/3, suspicious for primary or secondary malignancy.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and thorax confirmed a voluminous right thyroid mass and detected two pulmonary nodules consistent with metastases. MRI showed no lymphadenopathy. Laryngoscopy demonstrated freely mobile vocal cords.

clinical_record:
A 74-year-old man with a history of interstitial pneumonia presented with one month of right-sided chest pain that worsened with inspiration and severe sweating confined to his right arm and thoracic area, accompanied by a cold sensation. He denied abnormal sensation or muscle weakness. Six months earlier, chest CT had shown dense infiltrates in the ventral subpleural regions of the right upper and middle lobes; on admission these shadows had enlarged. Oral antibiotic therapy failed to improve the infiltrates, and he was admitted for further evaluation.

On examination, he was sweating profusely on the right arm and right thorax. Vital signs were blood pressure 150/78 mmHg, pulse 71/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. A pleural friction rub was heard over the right chest. The skin on the right arm, chest, and back was moister and cooler than the left. Thermography revealed decreased surface temperature over the right arm and right thorax corresponding to dermatomes C5–T12. Pupils were equal and reactive; eyelids were not droopy. Neurological examination showed no sensory deficits or abnormal reflexes.

He had no history of smoking, trauma, or asbestos exposure. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and varicose veins, treated with candesartan and ezetimibe. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9,000/μL and C-reactive protein of 1.14 mg/dL. Intravenous antibiotics were started on admission, but his symptoms, inflammatory markers, and imaging findings did not improve. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed macrophages 65.1%, lymphocytes 4.8%, neutrophils 29.9%, and eosinophils 0.2%, with no microorganisms or malignant cells. A transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy or specific inflammation.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: dense infiltrates in the ventral subpleural regions of the right upper and middle lobes
reviewer_a.missing_or_conflicting_component: specific tumor type (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma)
reviewer_a.reason: The patient presents with symptoms (right-sided chest pain, sweating confined to right arm/thoracic area, cold sensation, pleural friction rub, decreased surface temperature) and imaging findings (enlarging dense infiltrates in the right upper and middle lobes) highly suggestive of a Pancoast tumor. However, the specific etiology (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma) is not confirmed by biopsy.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: right-sided chest pain that worsened with inspiration and severe sweating confined to his right arm and thoracic area
reviewer_b.reason: Pancoast tumor is a plausible parent category for a superior sulcus lung cancer with Horner-like autonomic symptoms; it includes squamous cell carcinoma as a possible subtype but does not specify histology. It lacks the specific histologic subtype of the reference.

A 36-year-old G5P2+2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries and two first-trimester miscarriages was referred at 6 weeks of amenorrhea for evaluation of a pregnancy of unknown location. Her serum quantitative β-hCG was 16,124 mIU/mL. A transabdominal ultrasound at presentation did not locate an intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy. A copper intrauterine device had been removed 2 months before her last menstrual period. She had used one cycle of clomiphene. She had no chronic illnesses, did not smoke or drink, and was not on medications.

On examination, blood pressure was 113/70 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, and temperature 37.5 °C. Abdominal, cardiorespiratory, neurological, and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 13 mm gestational sac with irregular margins and a yolk sac in the anterior isthmic portion of the uterus, raising suspicion for a cesarean-section scar ectopic pregnancy. Doppler was declined. Serial β-hCG measurements rose by 33% over 48 hours (21,521 mIU/mL). The patient missed follow-up and returned 1 week later with 5 days of worsening pelvic pain.

Repeat transvaginal scan revealed a fetal pole with cardiac activity (crown–rump length 0.9 cm) in a sac traversing the full width of the anterior myometrium, extending exophytically toward the serosa, with trophoblastic flow on Doppler; there was no endometrial fluid or free pelvic fluid. She was taken to laparoscopy and hysteroscopy: the bladder was densely adherent to the anterior uterine wall, the ectopic was not visualized, and extensive intrauterine adhesions obscured the view; there was no intracavitary bleeding. Postoperatively, she became hypotensive (systolic 82–95 mmHg) without vaginal bleeding. This prompted an urgent MRI to map the location of the pregnancy.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.reason: This candidate is a complete equivalent of the reference diagnosis, with 'cesarean-section' being a common synonym for 'cesarean'.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: raising suspicion for a cesarean-section scar ectopic pregnancy
reviewer_b.reason: Synonymous wording for the same diagnostic entity; no clinical difference.

A 35-year-old man from rural north India presented with a one-month history of a progressively enlarging, central abdominal lump. Three weeks after the lump appeared, he developed intermittent high-grade fever and dull, aching abdominal pain. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, there was a moderately tender mass in the umbilical region. There was non-tender thickening of the right spermatic cord without scrotal or testicular abnormalities; inguinal nodes were barely palpable, and there was no lower-extremity edema. Complete blood counts and blood chemistry were within normal limits, and blood cultures were sterile. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large, well-defined, unilocular cyst measuring 20 × 14 × 23 cm located behind the right colon and terminal ileum, without features suggestive of an abscess; the remainder of the abdominal organs appeared normal. Contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed these findings but did not clarify the origin or etiology of the cyst. Because of diagnostic uncertainty and ongoing symptoms, the abdomen was explored surgically, revealing a large retroperitoneal cyst posterior to the right colon, mesocolon, and terminal ileum that stretched adjacent structures; a well-defined avascular plane allowed complete excision of the cyst, and a conglomeration of grossly dilated lymphatics near its upper pole was also removed.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: a large retroperitoneal cyst posterior to the right colon, mesocolon, and terminal ileum that stretched adjacent structures; a well-defined avascular plane allowed complete excision of the cyst, and a conglomeration of grossly dilated lymphatics near its upper pole was also removed.
reviewer_a.reason: The record describes a retroperitoneal cyst and 'grossly dilated lymphatics', which is consistent with a retroperitoneal lymphatic malformation.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: a large retroperitoneal cyst posterior to the right colon, mesocolon, and terminal ileum
reviewer_b.reason: Retroperitoneal lymphatic malformation is a broader term that could encompass the described findings, but it does not specify the filarial etiology.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of fever and rapidly progressive fullness in the throat, pain on swallowing, dysphagia, and dyspnea. On examination, there was local redness at the root of the tongue but no other mucosal inflammation. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with a left shift and elevated C-reactive protein; thyroid-stimulating hormone, triiodothyronine, and thyroxine levels were normal. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a non-homogeneous, mass-like prominence at the base of the tongue compressing the epiglottis and narrowing the pharynx. Neck ultrasound failed to identify the thyroid gland in its normal pretracheal location. Contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrated a 1.7 cm non-homogeneous, contrast-enhancing area at the tongue base with peripheral calcifications; several adjacent 1 cm nodular structures enhanced similarly to thyroid tissue, and no thyroid gland was seen in the usual neck location.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.reason: This candidate is a common and equivalent way to refer to the reference diagnosis.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: mass-like prominence at the base of the tongue
reviewer_b.reason: Synonymous with lingual thyroid gland.

A 61-year-old man with a 20-year history of recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, bloating, and obstipation, alternating with intermittent diarrhea, and a 30-lb weight loss presented for evaluation. His history included heavy alcohol use (12–24 beers daily for 20 years) and an uncomplicated cholecystectomy 10 years earlier, after which symptoms began eight days postoperatively. Over the next decade, colonoscopy and esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed no abnormalities, “including any evidence of celiac disease.” A trial of conservative management failed, and exploratory laparotomy “showed no mechanical cause of the obstructions.” Alcohol use stopped 2 years ago because of worsening symptoms. Fifteen months after the first surgery, a CT scan showed small-bowel dilation (approximately 23 mm in diameter) consistent with obstruction and a concurrent megacolon dilated up to 15 cm. Laboratory studies revealed low levels of fat-soluble vitamins: vitamin A 22 µg/dL (reference, 32.5–78.0), vitamin D 7 ng/mL (20–50), vitamin E 4.3 mg/L (5.5–17), and vitamin K 2.65 ng/mL (0.23–3.2). A gluten-free diet trialed for 3 months produced no improvement.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: 20-year history of recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, bloating, and obstipation, alternating with intermittent diarrhea
reviewer_a.reason: The patient's 20-year history of recurrent symptoms, small-bowel dilation, and megacolon, with no mechanical obstruction found, strongly supports chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: small-bowel dilation ... consistent with obstruction and a concurrent megacolon
reviewer_b.reason: Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction is the clinical syndrome present, but it is a broader parent of brown bowel syndrome, which is a specific histopathologic cause.

A 25-year-old man with a history of Hodgkin lymphoma presented with a 2-month history of a gradually enlarging mass over the dorsum of his left hand. Six years earlier, he had been diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma on the basis of mediastinal lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms, and he received 13 courses of chemotherapy. Physical examination at this visit revealed a soft-tissue mass over the second metacarpal dorsum, approximately 4 cm in greatest dimension, with mild tenderness and no limitation of movement. The patient underwent surgical excision of the lesion, and two specimens were submitted to pathology. The larger specimen consisted of gray, gelatinous tissue measuring 4 × 2.5 × 0.8 cm and 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 cm. Microscopic examination showed a mixture of inflammatory cells, abundant myxoid stroma, epithelioid and spindle-shaped cells, lipoblast-like cells, and occasional Reed–Sternberg–like cells. Given the presence of Reed–Sternberg–like cells in an inflammatory background, the pathologist recommended immunohistochemical staining to distinguish among possible diagnoses.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.missing_or_conflicting_component: presence of lipoblast-like cells and Reed-Sternberg-like cells
reviewer_a.reason: Inflammatory myxohyaline tumor is a related entity but typically lacks the lipoblast-like cells and Reed-Sternberg-like cells seen in this case, which are characteristic of myxoinflammatory fibroblastic sarcoma.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: myxoid stroma, epithelioid and spindle-shaped cells
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Inflammatory myxohyaline tumor is a broader category that includes myxoinflammatory fibroblastic sarcoma; the specific subtype is not specified.
reviewer_b.reason: Inflammatory myxohyaline tumor is a broader term encompassing myxoinflammatory fibroblastic sarcoma, so it is a parent category rather than the exact diagnosis.

An 18-year-old man presented with 20 days of pain and swelling around his right scapula, which had been gradually increasing in size, and 2 days of fever. He had been receiving anti-tubercular therapy for presumed pulmonary tuberculosis for 6 months; the diagnosis had been based on cough, chest radiograph findings, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, with negative sputum studies. Despite continued therapy, 3 days before presentation he developed swelling and pain of the left ankle with difficulty walking. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 73 mm/h and a positive C-reactive protein level of 96 mg/L. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder and left ankle demonstrated findings consistent with osteomyelitis involving the scapula and the distal tibia. An aspiration of the scapular swelling was performed, and specimens were sent for culture, sensitivity testing, and histopathologic examination for possible multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.

reviewer_a.reason: The record strongly suggests tuberculous osteomyelitis based on the patient's history of presumed pulmonary tuberculosis, ongoing anti-tubercular therapy, and new osteomyelitis findings. However, this candidate does not specify the affected anatomical sites (scapula and distal tibia) as identified in the MRI.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: possible multidrug-resistant tuberculosis
reviewer_b.reason: Tuberculosis is a suspected differential, not the reference cryptococcal osteomyelitis.

He had been receiving anti-tubercular therapy for presumed pulmonary tuberculosis for 6 months; the diagnosis had been based on cough, chest radiograph findings, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, with negative sputum studies. Despite continued therapy, 3 days before presentation he developed swelling and pain of the left ankle with difficulty walking. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 73 mm/h and a positive C-reactive protein level of 96 mg/L. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder and left ankle demonstrated findings consistent with osteomyelitis involving the scapula and the distal tibia. An aspiration of the scapular swelling was performed, and specimens were sent for culture, sensitivity testing, and histopathologic examination for possible multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.

reviewer_a.reason: Skeletal tuberculosis is a broader category that includes osteomyelitis. The record specifically identifies osteomyelitis of the scapula and distal tibia. This candidate is a parent term and lacks the specific anatomical detail.

reviewer_b.reason: Skeletal tuberculosis is a differential, not the reference cryptococcal osteomyelitis.

A 14-year-old boy was referred from a mission hospital for postoperative wound sepsis after right scrotal exploration and orchidectomy for testicular torsion. He had 24 h of scrotal pain and swelling before surgery. On arrival he was tachypneic, tachycardic (124 bpm), febrile (38.7 °C), and diaphoretic, with pallor of mucous membranes. Blood pressure was 109/68 mmHg, neck veins were flat, and heart sounds were normal. The tips of his fingers and toes appeared cyanosed bilaterally with peripheral oxygen saturations fluctuating between 20% and 30% on room air, despite no severe dyspnea. Ecchymoses were present over the extremities, and he bled easily from puncture sites. The right groin wound appeared necrotic and septic. He had no chronic illnesses or medications and denied smoking.  

Initial laboratory studies showed white blood cells 16 × 10^3/µL with neutrophils 10.8 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 4.8 g/dL, and platelets 26 × 10^3/µL; liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, malaria smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis were normal. A diagnosis of severe sepsis complicated by DIC and anemia was made, and he received broad-spectrum antibiotics, blood and platelet transfusions, and surgical debridement.  

Despite improvement in systemic parameters and extubation on day 6, cyanosis of fingers and toes progressed to well-demarcated gangrene below the elbows and knees. A contrast angiogram of the aorta and its branches showed patent thoracic and abdominal aorta and no filling defects in major limb arteries.

reviewer_a.reason: Purpura fulminans is a severe, acute, and often fatal thrombotic disorder characterized by rapidly progressive hemorrhagic necrosis of the skin, often associated with DIC. An 86-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of skin lesions on his abdomen and lower back. He reported occasional blurry vision and joint aches but denied weight loss, chills, abdominal pain, bleeding, or healing problems. His medical history was notable only for a 20–pack-year smoking history (quit 50 years ago) and no history of skin cancer. On examination, there were numerous moderately severe, irregular, erythematous papules and nodules on the abdomen and lower back. C-reactive protein was elevated at 19.5 mg/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 249 U/L. A panel for sexually transmitted infections was negative. A shave biopsy of a representative papule revealed in the dermis a dense infiltrate of monotonous neoplastic cells with dispersed chromatin and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.

A 60-year-old man with a 14-year history of polycythemia vera and hypertension was admitted with acute severe abdominal pain, nausea, and transient loss of consciousness. He reported vague abdominal discomfort intermittently over the past decade. His medications included aspirin, hydroxyurea, and intermittent losartan; he had poor adherence to phlebotomies and other therapy. On arrival, blood pressure was 110/75 mmHg; he was lethargic and confused. Physical examination showed epigastric and periumbilical tenderness, splenomegaly, and left costovertebral-angle tenderness. An abdominopelvic CT scan with contrast demonstrated splenomegaly and a 40 × 23 mm hypodense lesion in the right adrenal gland (55 HU) and a 60 × 35 mm ill-defined lesion in the left adrenal gland, without evidence of vascular thrombosis. Two days later, after supportive care, an adrenal-protocol CT showed persistent massive splenomegaly (25 cm) and bilateral adrenal masses (right 40 × 29 mm, left 48 × 26 mm) that were nonenhancing with an attenuation of 50 HU.

An 84-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, irritable bowel syndrome, transient ischemic attack, lung cancer with bone metastases, and bilateral knee osteoarthritis presented for evaluation of right knee pain and increased back pain. He had been treated for brucellosis 5 years earlier. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There was a 5 × 10 cm soft, fluctuant, non-tender mass in the posterior aspect of the right knee without erythema, warmth, or discharge. Knee range of motion was full, and distal neurovascular status was intact. Laboratory studies showed a low white-cell count and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Ultrasonography of the right knee demonstrated a moderate to large joint effusion without definite synovial thickening. On August 22, ultrasound-guided aspiration of the posterior knee swelling yielded 80 mL of fluid, which was sent for culture and cell‐count analysis.

reviewer_b.reason: Septic arthritis is a broader category that could include brucellar infection, but the specific etiology is not established.

A 47-year-old woman reported a 1-year history of persistent foreign body sensation in her right eye unrelieved by sodium hyaluronate drops. She had no personal or family history of systemic diseases, including multiple myeloma, neurologic or autoimmune disorders, and no history of dialysis.  
On examination, visual acuity and intraocular pressure were normal. A linear, soft-tissue lesion was noted centrally along the lower conjunctival fornix of the right eye; the mass appeared pinkish-yellow rather than the typical salmon pink of lymphoid lesions.  
Orbital computed tomography demonstrated a purely conjunctival, homogeneous mass isodense to muscle without infiltration of adjacent structures.  
Routine blood tests, including complete blood count and serum chemistry, were unremarkable.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_b.decisive_span: pinkish-yellow rather than the typical salmon pink of lymphoid lesions
reviewer_b.reason: Conjunctival fibroma is a different benign tumor; the clinical and imaging features are more consistent with amyloidosis, and fibroma is not a typical differential in this presentation.

A 78-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 4-year history of progressive gait disturbance characterized by imbalance, slow walking, and repeated falls, accompanied initially by a head tremor. One year after onset, she developed recent memory impairment and occasional psychotic episodes. Over the subsequent years, her walking disability worsened to a rigid-akinetic syndrome requiring support for ambulation, and she eventually became wheelchair-bound. Nonmotor symptoms included reduced speech output, impaired comprehension, emotional lability, and dependency in daily activities.  

On brain MRI performed in 2022, there was diffuse, generalized hyperintensity of the supratentorial white matter on T2/FLAIR sequences involving all cerebral lobes. No contrast enhancement was seen on T1 postgadolinium images, and diffusion-weighted imaging showed no areas of restricted diffusion.  

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a mildly elevated protein concentration of 56.6 mg/dL (reference range, 15–45 mg/dL), with a normal cell count (0 cells/mm3) and glucose level (59 mg/dL). Tests for KOH, bacterioscopy, culture, cytology, and JC virus in the CSF were negative.

While the patient has gait disturbance and cognitive decline, the clinical presentation and MRI findings do not specifically align with CBD. The diffuse white matter hyperintensities are not typical for CBD.

reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: CBD typically has asymmetric cortical atrophy, not diffuse white matter disease
reviewer_b.reason: CBD presents with asymmetric parkinsonism and cortical signs; diffuse white matter involvement is not typical.

A 60-year-old woman presented with progressive hoarseness and shortness of breath over 2 months. Fourteen years earlier, she had undergone resection of a laryngeal tumour, which was diagnosed as chondroma. She has long-standing hypertension, does not smoke or drink, and has no family history of malignancy. On examination, an approximately 6-cm, fixed, oval-shaped mass was palpated on the left side of the neck, with no palpable lymphadenopathy. Indirect laryngoscopy showed displacement and immobility of the left hemilarynx and reduced respiratory space; the mucosa was intact. Laboratory tests were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 5.6-cm, hypodense mass containing calcifications in the left subglottic laryngeal wall, with infiltration and partial destruction of the cricoid and thyroid cartilages and significant subglottic luminal narrowing. No pathologic lymphadenopathy or distant metastases were identified on chest x-ray or abdominal ultrasound.

reviewer_a.reason: The record strongly suggests chondrosarcoma based on imaging and clinical progression, and the location is specified as laryngeal. However, without histopathology, it's not a definitive diagnosis.

A 68-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of hemoptysis and a 1-month history of mild cough, sputum production, and rhinorrhea. Her past medical history was unremarkable, with no malignancy, immunosuppressive therapy, diabetes mellitus, or vasculitis. On examination, vital signs were normal. Mild wheezing was auscultated bilaterally; neurologic and skin findings were normal. Laboratory tests showed an elevated C-reactive protein level of 7 mg/dL (reference: 0–0.3 mg/dL) and a normal white-cell count with a neutrophil count of 3.97 × 10^3/μL. HIV testing was negative. Initial microbiologic studies—including bacterial cultures, acid-fast bacillus smear and culture of sputum, blood cultures (bacterial and fungal), and respiratory viral serologies—were all negative. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated multiple nodules and masses of various sizes in both lung fields, some with cavitation. Chest CT (lung window) showed cavitary and noncavitary nodules and masses with faint surrounding ground-glass opacity (“halo sign”). Cavitary lesions had thick, irregular walls with septa-like structures; on mediastinal windows, one lesion contained a hypoattenuating area. A coronal maximum intensity projection image showed patent vessels within the lesions. A small bilateral pleural effusion was present. 

Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody titers (both c-ANCA and p-ANCA) were within normal limits. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy revealed diffuse granulomatous inflammation but no organisms. Video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection of a cavitary lesion was performed. Histopathologic analysis showed diffuse necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and fungal elements. Methenamine silver staining revealed yeast-like structures associated with septate hyphae demonstrating acute-angle branching.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: Methenamine silver staining revealed yeast-like structures associated with septate hyphae demonstrating acute-angle branching.
reviewer_a.reason: The histopathology describes septate hyphae with acute-angle branching, which is characteristic of Aspergillus. The clinical presentation (immunocompetent patient, cavitary lesions, halo sign) is also compatible with invasive aspergillosis, although the patient is not explicitly immunocompromised, which is a common risk factor. However, the record does not definitively identify Aspergillus over other molds with similar morphology, nor does it rule out Fusarium.

reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Aspergillus typically shows septate hyphae with acute-angle branching but not yeast-like structures; Fusarium is the correct genus.
reviewer_b.reason: Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis is a related mold infection but the presence of yeast-like structures points to Fusarium, not Aspergillus.

A 78-year-old woman with a history of two prior catheter ablations for persistent atrial fibrillation—initial pulmonary vein isolation followed six months later by repeat pulmonary vein reisolation, complex fractionated electrogram ablation, and linear lesions across the left atrial roof and mitral isthmus—presented with palpitations. clinical_record:
A 53-year-old man was admitted for progressive dyspnea (NYHA class III). His history included a congenital ventricular septal defect repaired in childhood, subsequent aortic valve and septal patch replacements, permanent atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, chronic hepatitis C–related liver disease, and prior admission for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. On examination, he had jugular venous distension, irregular rhythm, a 2/6 systolic murmur at the aortic and mitral areas, decreased breath sounds at the right lung base, and peripheral edema.  
ECG showed atrial fibrillation with left bundle branch block. Chest radiography demonstrated pulmonary congestion and a right basal pleural effusion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed: a dilated left ventricle with preserved ejection fraction (60%), a dilated right ventricle with normal systolic function, no residual septal shunt, a normally functioning mechanical aortic prosthesis but elevated transprosthetic gradients (mean 33 mmHg) with an effective orifice area index of 0.4 cm2/m2 (suggesting severe prosthesis–patient mismatch), moderate mitral regurgitation, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 50 mmHg. The inferior vena cava was dilated with poor inspiratory collapse.  
An initial diagnosis of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction was made, and intravenous diuretics led to reduction of edema and resolution of radiographic congestion, but the patient remained dyspneic with low exercise tolerance and still required supplemental oxygen.  
A contrast CT scan of the chest and abdomen showed a small right pleural effusion, no lung parenchymal disease or pulmonary embolism, cirrhotic liver with a focal lesion suspicious for hepatocellular carcinoma, splenomegaly, and signs of portal hypertension.  
Right heart catheterization revealed a high cardiac output state, normal pulmonary vascular resistance, and only a slight elevation of mean pulmonary and wedge pressures.

A 61-year-old woman with cervical cancer metastatic to paraaortic and left supraclavicular lymph nodes was treated with systemic chemotherapy: paclitaxel and bevacizumab administered for 63 and 36 days before presentation, respectively, each followed the next day by cisplatin. A 35-year-old woman presented with a 15-month history of vaginal bleeding and intermittent sensation of a mass in the vagina. She described bleeding with clots every 1–2 weeks lasting 2–5 days without a separate menstrual cycle; between bleeding episodes she had a watery, nonfoul-smelling vaginal discharge and occasional postcoital bleeding. She denied dyspnea, palpitations, or bleeding from other sites. Her obstetric history included three home vaginal deliveries; she underwent minilaparotomy sterilization 11 years prior and tubal recanalization 5 years ago. Prior evaluations—including coagulation studies, pelvic ultrasonography, and empiric therapy with progesterone, tranexamic acid, and antibiotics—had not alleviated her symptoms.

On examination she appeared pale but hemodynamically stable. Abdominal exam was unremarkable. On bimanual pelvic examination there was a firm, globular 6×4 cm mass within the vaginal canal; a separate cervical os could not be identified and the uterine fundus was not palpable. Active vaginal bleeding was noted. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.3 g/dL with normal platelet count and PT/INR. Pelvic ultrasonography—performed multiple times, including in the preoperative area—was reported as normal and was unable to clarify the origin of the mass. Magnetic resonance imaging was not available. After resuscitation with intravenous fluids and two units of whole blood, she was scheduled for emergency surgical management.

A 63-year-old white man presented with a 3-week history of redness of the left eye and extensive bilateral lymphadenopathy. He reported blurred vision and loss of vision in the left lower quadrant, with supraorbital pain in both eyes, all worsening over 3 weeks. A 48-year-old postmenopausal woman (gravida 2, para 2) presented with a 3-month history of brown-yellowish vaginal discharge, fluctuating lower abdominal pain, fever, and progressive abdominal enlargement over 15 years, worsening in the last 5 years. There was no relevant drug or family history.

An 18-year-old African male with no prior medical history presented first with a 2-day history of tonsillitis and a new macular rash on his chest that extended to his arms. Three days later he developed abdominal cramping and multiple episodes of non-bloody, watery diarrhea without nausea or vomiting, along with fevers and joint pains in his wrists, elbows, and knees. Initial outpatient care included oral chlorhexidine, lozenges, and symptomatic treatment.

He was then seen at a local health facility with high fever, tachycardia, and within 24 hours became confused with rising serum creatinine (from 200 to 400 μmol/L). He received ceftriaxone, paracetamol, loperamide, and one dose of IV methylprednisolone, but continued to deteriorate and was transferred to our hospital.

On arrival he was febrile (40°C), hypotensive (70/40 mmHg), tachycardic (130 bpm), tachypneic (50 breaths/min), and hypoxemic (SaO2 86% on room air). GCS was 14/15. Lung exam revealed bilaterally coarse crepitations; cardiovascular exam an audible S3 gallop; abdomen distended and tense with hypoactive bowel sounds; musculoskeletal exam was normal. He received fluid resuscitation, central line placement, and norepinephrine at 0.4 μg/kg/min.

Laboratory data showed: WBC 27.1×10^9/L; Hb 10.9 g/dL; platelets 281×10^9/L; procalcitonin 71.6 ng/mL; CRP 287 mg/L; creatinine 494 μmol/L; urea 26.7 mmol/L; Na 128 mmol/L; K 4.87 mmol/L; HCO3– 15.5 mmol/L; blood gas pH 7.33, PCO2 23 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3– 19.8 mmol/L. Liver tests showed AST 1461 U/L and ALT 812 U/L; hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV screens were negative. Urinalysis had 3+ protein and 4+ blood without RBCs; urine albumin:creatinine ratio was 52.3 mg/mmol. Cardiac markers were elevated (troponin 17 137 ng/mL; CK > 7800 U/L).

A negative ASOT made rheumatic fever unlikely. Chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly; echocardiogram revealed dilated cardiomyopathy with EF 30–35% and normal valves. Abdominal CT demonstrated a distended bowel with splenic and renal infarcts. HRCT confirmed cardiomegaly with bi-basal atelectasis. Initial differentials included bacterial septic shock, vasculitis (antiphospholipid syndrome or medium-sized vessel vasculitis), and multisystem inflammatory syndrome.

He required intubation and increasing norepinephrine (0.7 μg/kg/min), meropenem, vancomycin, urgent dialysis, and cooling measures. An autoimmune panel showed low C3 (0.51 g/L) and C4 (0.04 g/L), and he received a low-dose steroid pulse (250 mg IV daily). Autoantibodies returned with a positive beta2-glycoprotein IgA antiphospholipid antibody and negative ANA, anti–dsDNA, ENA, pANCA, and cANCA. SARS-CoV-2 PCR from tracheal aspirate and nasal swab was negative.

A 29-year-old Caucasian man with a history of hepatitis C, posttraumatic stress disorder, polysubstance abuse, and tobacco use was brought to the emergency department after being found agitated and erratically wandering the streets and then unresponsive with multiple skin abrasions. Laboratory studies on admission showed features of severe rhabdomyolysis. Serologic testing confirmed chronic hepatitis C but was otherwise unremarkable. Serum toxicology tests were negative for ethanol, acetaminophen, and salicylates. Noncontrast CT of the head, MRI of the cervical spine, EEG, and chest and abdominal radiographs were normal. Right upper-quadrant ultrasonography revealed gallbladder calculi, a normal pancreatic duct, and an echogenic right kidney with prominent corticomedullary differentiation.

He received aggressive IV fluids, a norepinephrine infusion, and a bolus of amiodarone. Hyperkalemia was treated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, calcium gluconate, insulin with glucose, and IV bicarbonate. For severe hyperthermia, he was given dantrolene and placed on cooling blankets. He was sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated, and received rasburicase for hyperuricemia. A 46-year-old woman presented with right flank pain, dysuria, and hematuria. Her past medical history was notable for an abdominal hysterectomy 15 years earlier. General and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Urinalysis showed 6–8 red blood cells and 4–6 pus cells per high-power field but no other abnormalities.

An ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a focal hypoechoic polypoidal lesion measuring 3.4 × 2.8 cm along the anterosuperior wall of the urinary bladder, containing tiny hyperechoic foci; the outline of the adjacent bladder wall appeared indistinct. The uterus was not visualized; a cystic area was noted in the left adnexa, and both ovaries were not seen.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-defined soft-tissue–density lesion with calcific specks along the anterosuperior bladder wall that demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement in the early arterial and venous phases. The intraluminal component merged with the bladder wall, causing minimal localized wall thickening; the rest of the bladder wall was normal. Additional findings included a right calyceal calculus with mild pelvicalyceal dilatation, a simple right renal cyst, no pelvic lymphadenopathy, and left hydrosalpinx.

An 82-year-old man with epithelioid pleural mesothelioma (cT1N0M0) was treated with ipilimumab and nivolumab. After eight courses, follow-up chest CT showed new bilateral infiltrative shadows. He reported fever and dyspnea. Laboratory tests revealed elevated C-reactive protein and surfactant protein D levels; Krebs von den Lungen-6 was normal. Sputum cultures, procalcitonin, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR were negative. Serologic testing for anti–nuclear antigen, anti–aminoacyl–tRNA synthetase, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide, anti-Sjögren’s-syndrome-related antigen A and B, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antigen antibodies were all negative. He had no history of antigen exposure. Immunotherapy was discontinued. He received lascufloxacin and then tazobactam/ceftolozane without improvement; oxygen requirement increased to 2 L/min. Based on the clinical picture and imaging, grade 3 ICI-induced pneumonitis was suspected. He underwent methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days followed by prednisolone 60 mg/day for 8 days, but chest radiographs remained unchanged and oxygen needs rose to 4 L/min. A second course of methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days produced no clinical improvement. One week later, bronchoscopy showed no airway secretions. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained 29% neutrophils, 58% lymphocytes, 13% macrophages, and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.33. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy, and cultures of bronchoscopy specimens were negative. Based on these findings, he was diagnosed with steroid-refractory ICI-induced pneumonitis.

reviewer_a.reason: This candidate is a compatible child of the reference, as ICI-induced pneumonitis is a type of immune-related pneumonitis. However, the record provides further specificity regarding steroid refractoriness.

A 76-year-old woman with a history of appendicitis, torsion of an ovarian cyst pedicle, and uterine myoma presented with a rapidly enlarging right parietal mass behind the ear over one month. Intraoperatively, the tumor was extradural, caused skull destruction, and had no intradural involvement. Initial evaluations showed lactic acid 0.7 mmol/L, blood ketones <0.2 mmol/L, salicylate <0.4 mmol/L, and unchanged renal function insufficient to explain the degree of acidosis. An 8‐year‐old boy with no significant past medical history presented with a 30-minute history of generalized abdominal pain followed by a single episode of vomiting. During the event he developed diaphoresis, mucocutaneous paleness, dizziness, dysarthria, incoherent speech, and lack of eye contact, without loss of consciousness, abnormal movements, or sphincter relaxation. The episode lasted 10 minutes, after which he reported a frontal headache (5/10) and persistent nausea. Family denied toxin or medication exposure. He had a similar episode 18 months earlier, diagnosed as migraine. There was no personal or family history of epilepsy or neurological disorders. Developmental milestones were age‐appropriate, and he was performing well in school.

On admission, his vital signs were normal except for blood pressure above the 95th percentile for age. Neurologic examination revealed confusion and disorientation; he could not recognize his mother or speak but could follow visual commands. Motor and sensory examinations were normal. Approximately 20 minutes after arrival, his consciousness and orientation improved. Over the next hours he had three additional self‐limited vomiting episodes and ongoing headache, which improved after a single IV dose of diclofenac (1 mg/kg).

Complete blood count, serum chemistries, and electrolytes (including sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus) were all within normal limits. Brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol was reported as normal for age.

A 22-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of generalized painful fluid‐filled skin lesions, 7 days of yellow scleral discoloration, and 1 month of fever following removal of a tibial implant. Two years earlier, he had sustained a tibial fracture treated with internal fixation. After implant removal, he developed a surgical-site infection and persistent fever; he initially took paracetamol without relief, then obtained ciprofloxacin over the counter. Two days after starting ciprofloxacin, he developed generalized pruritus that progressed to fluid-filled rashes. He denied angioedema, dyspnea, abdominal distention, lower-limb swelling, hematemesis, melena, altered sensorium, alcohol use, or immunocompromise.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. He had icterus but no pallor, clubbing, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, or dehydration. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed multiple generalized vesicles and bullae with non-hemorrhagic crusts over the trunk and extremities (palms and soles spared). Lesions were tender, with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Mucosal findings included hemorrhagic lip crusts and penile erosion.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Leukocyte count 18,520/mm3 (neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 22%, eosinophils 12%)  
• Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 423,000/mm3  
• AST 283 U/L, ALT 246 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1390 U/L  
• Total bilirubin 14 mg/dL (conjugated 13.7 mg/dL)  
• Albumin 2.4 g/dL, INR 2.7  
• Renal function and electrolytes were within normal limits.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: eosinophils 12%
reviewer_a.missing_or_conflicting_component: The full criteria for DRESS syndrome are not explicitly met or ruled out, but eosinophilia and systemic symptoms are present.
reviewer_a.reason: DRESS syndrome is a type of severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR) characterized by rash, fever, eosinophilia, and internal organ involvement. The patient presents with fever, generalized fluid-filled skin lesions, eosinophilia (12%), and significant liver injury (AST 283 U/L, ALT 246 U/L, ALP 1390 U/L, total bilirubin 14 mg/dL). This is highly suggestive of DRESS, which is a broader category than TEN.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: generalized painful fluid-filled skin lesions
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: DRESS requires eosinophilia and systemic symptoms; here eosinophilia is only 12% and no organ involvement beyond skin; TEN is the primary diagnosis.
reviewer_b.reason: DRESS is a distinct drug reaction with fever, rash, eosinophilia, and internal organ involvement; the case lacks the characteristic eosinophilia and systemic features, and the skin findings are more consistent with TEN.

clinical_record:
A 74-year-old right-handed woman was brought to the psychiatry clinic with a 5-month history of abrupt onset of disorganized speech, severe anxiety, and self-harm behaviors that began after a family trip. Her speech was rapid, fluent, and nonsensical—exemplified by the phrase “Our neighbor has gone to the cobbler to buy Ghormeh Sabzi”—consistent with Wernicke’s aphasia. Over the ensuing months, she developed agitation, persecutory delusions, visual and auditory hallucinations, urinary and fecal incontinence, and a persistent urge to flee her home.

Her psychiatric history included a 10-year history of depression treated with sertraline. There was no prior cognitive impairment or neurological disease. On examination, she was disoriented to time, demonstrated anomia, and had marked perseveration on the Clock Drawing Test, impaired performance on Luria’s three-step test, and defective crossed-pentagon drawing. Cognitive testing revealed an MMSE score of 2/30 and an ACE-R score of 2/100, likely confounded by comprehension deficits.

An initial brain MRI performed 2 months after symptom onset was reported as normal. She was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and started on memantine and quetiapine, without clinical improvement. Because of the acute presentation and prominent frontal and temporal features, she was referred to neurology for further assessment.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: prominent frontal and temporal features
reviewer_a.reason: The patient's presentation with disorganized speech, severe anxiety, self-harm behaviors, agitation, persecutory delusions, and prominent frontal and temporal features is highly suggestive of a frontotemporal dementia spectrum disorder. However, the specific subtype (e.g., behavioral variant FTD, primary progressive aphasia) is not explicitly stated or fully characterized to the level of a specific diagnosis.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: prominent frontal and temporal features
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Acute onset and incontinence are atypical for FTD.
reviewer_b.reason: FTD is a differential due to frontal/temporal features but is not the reference and lacks typical insidious course.

clinical_record:
A 15-year-old male presented with a 4-week history of watery diarrhea (20 episodes per day), vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain aggravated by spicy foods. He reported an 8-kg weight loss (≈15% of body weight). Physical examination revealed brownish macules on the hands and feet, hyperchromic punctate lesions on the trunk, and onychodystrophy. His medical history was notable for cleft lip and palate repair and recurrent diarrheal episodes since childhood.

Laboratory studies demonstrated mild hypoproteinemia and hypoalbuminemia (total protein 3.52 g/dL [normal 6.6–8.3], albumin 2.09 g/dL [3.5–5.2]), zinc deficiency (51 µg/dL [70–120]), low vitamin B12 (<150 pg/mL [300–900]), and otherwise unremarkable blood counts and metabolic panel.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed multiple type II and III Yamada polyps on atrophic gastric mucosa and nodular lymphoid lesions in the duodenum. Colonoscopy revealed numerous sessile and subpedunculated polyps throughout the colon and rectum.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: multiple type II and III Yamada polyps on atrophic gastric mucosa and nodular lymphoid lesions in the duodenum. Colonoscopy revealed numerous sessile and subpedunculated polyps throughout the colon and rectum.
reviewer_a.reason: Juvenile polyposis syndrome is characterized by juvenile polyps, typically in the colon. The record describes various types of polyps (Yamada polyps, sessile, subpedunculated) but does not specify their histological type as 'juvenile polyps'. The presence of ectodermal changes also points away from isolated juvenile polyposis.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: numerous sessile and subpedunculated polyps throughout the colon and rectum
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Juvenile polyposis syndrome is a polyposis syndrome but lacks the ectodermal changes and nutritional deficiencies characteristic of Cronkhite-Canada syndrome.
reviewer_b.reason: Juvenile polyposis syndrome shares the gastrointestinal polyposis component but is a distinct hereditary syndrome without the ectodermal features.

clinical_record:
A 33-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-month history of progressively worsening occipital headache, exacerbated by Valsalva maneuvers. On neurologic examination, he had bilateral past-pointing and an intention tremor. Brain MRI revealed a 6.9 × 5.5 × 6.1 cm lobulated mass centered at the left cerebellopontine angle, extending craniocaudally from the left ambient cistern to the premedullary space. The lesion involved and expanded Meckel’s cave, with a small extension into the left infratemporal fossa via the foramen ovale. It contained multiloculated T1-hypointense, T2-FLAIR–partially suppressible nonenhancing cystic areas with interspersed enhancing septa, as well as T1/T2-isointense enhancing solid components. Susceptibility-weighted imaging demonstrated curvilinear signal loss with corresponding T1 hyperintensity consistent with hemorrhagic foci, and diffusion-weighted imaging showed no diffusion restriction. There was compression of the left cerebellum and brainstem, dilation of the third, fourth, and lateral ventricles, anterior displacement of the cavernous sinus, and encasement with mild narrowing of the left petrous internal carotid artery; the masticator muscles were preserved. Noncontrast CT of the head showed smooth remodeling and erosion of the left petrous apex, clivus, carotid canal, and foramen ovale, along with two punctate calcifications; the internal auditory canals and inner ear structures were unremarkable.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: involved and expanded Meckel’s cave
reviewer_a.reason: Chordomas typically arise from notochordal remnants, often in the clivus or sacrum, and do not typically involve Meckel's cave in this manner.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: smooth remodeling and erosion of the left petrous apex, clivus, carotid canal, and foramen ovale
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: Chordoma typically shows destructive bone changes and is midline; this lesion is centered at CPA with Meckel's cave involvement and no diffusion restriction, favoring schwannoma.
reviewer_b.reason: Chordoma is a different entity with different imaging characteristics and location; the findings are more consistent with trigeminal schwannoma.

clinical_record:
A 41-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 2-year history of progressively worsening fever, weight loss, night sweats, and a dry cough. He also reported chronic lower back pain without neurologic deficits and a painful nonhealing ulcer on his right hallux. He had two sputum GeneXpert tests at local clinics, both negative. He was treated symptomatically with paracetamol, NSAIDs, and topical antibacterials.  

On referral for the toe ulcer, examination revealed a cachectic man who was normotensive and afebrile, with no lymphadenopathy or edema. He had tenderness over the thoracic spine but no neurologic deficits. Laboratory tests showed:  
• Hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, white cells 7.3×10^9/L, platelets 369×10^9/L  
• ESR >130 mm/hr, CRP 113 mg/L  
• IgA 6.2 g/L, anti-DNase B 259 IU/mL  
• Negative ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA, HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis serologies  
• Urine protein-creatinine ratio 0.242 g/mmol; dipstick: 3+ leukocytes, 3+ red blood cells; microscopy: granular casts; urine culture: no growth  

Chest radiograph showed bilateral reticular-nodular opacities. An induced sputum was trace positive for MTB on GeneXpert and subsequently grew MTB sensitive to rifampicin and isoniazid. Biopsy of the toe ulcer showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with a solitary acid-fast bacillus. MRI of the spine revealed contiguous spondylitis from T6 to T10 with discitis and an epidural/paraspinal collection causing spinal cord compression. Renal ultrasound demonstrated normal-sized kidneys with increased echogenicity.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: Biopsy of the toe ulcer showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with a solitary acid-fast bacillus. MRI of the spine revealed contiguous spondylitis from T6 to T10 with discitis and an epidural/paraspinal collection causing spinal cord compression.
reviewer_a.reason: Extrapulmonary sites (toe ulcer, spine) are clearly involved, but there is also pulmonary involvement, making 'Extrapulmonary tuberculosis' an incomplete description of the overall disease burden.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: Biopsy of the toe ulcer showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with a solitary acid-fast bacillus
reviewer_b.reason: Extrapulmonary TB is a component of the overall TB presentation, but the case also has pulmonary TB, so it is not the complete final object.

A 58‐year‐old man presented to the emergency department with a 24‐hour history of right iliac fossa pain, nausea, and diarrhea. A 20-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of intermittent abdominal pain, recurrent vomiting, and melena. She had no significant past medical history and no family history of cancer. On examination, she had mild abdominal tenderness; gynecological examination was normal. Laboratory studies revealed iron-deficiency anemia; white blood cell and platelet counts were normal. Upper and lower endoscopies were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance enterography demonstrated a focal segment of small-bowel wall thickening measuring 15 mm by 2 mm. An exploratory laparotomy revealed an exophytic ileal mass with mesenteric lymphadenopathy but no peritoneal or hepatic metastases. A wide segmental resection was performed without complication.

Gross examination showed a 30 mm by 25 mm polypoid, tan-white, lobulated mass arising from the small-intestinal wall. Microscopically, the lesion was a transmural, infiltrative proliferation of uniform epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in nested and fascicular patterns, with variable eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm, round to oval vesicular nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and up to 10 mitoses per 10 high-power fields; there was mucosal ulceration but no melanin pigment, lymphovascular invasion, or perineural invasion, and three mesenteric lymph nodes were negative for tumor.

Immunohistochemical analysis showed diffuse, strong positivity for S100 protein and SOX10; HMB45 and Melan A were negative. There was patchy synaptophysin expression. CD117, DOG1, cytokeratin, CD34, smooth muscle actin, desmin, chromogranin, and CD56 were all negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.reason: This candidate is a broader diagnosis, missing the specific gastrointestinal location which is clearly identified in the record as an 'ileal mass'.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: S100 protein and SOX10; HMB45 and Melan A were negative
reviewer_b.reason: The immunophenotype and morphology are diagnostic of clear cell sarcoma of the gastrointestinal tract.

A 64-year-old white man was admitted in March 2016 with acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia. He had been on therapeutic anticoagulation for paroxysmal “pre-shimmering.” His history included two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, first noted in August 2015; biopsies at that time showed histologically proven adenoma without malignancy. On presentation, he was hemodynamically stable but had a hemoglobin level of 4.4 mmol/L. He reported no weight loss, fever, or constitutional symptoms. Laboratory studies showed α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels within normal ranges; serum human chorionic gonadotropin was not measured. Abdominal ultrasound revealed subcapsular hepatic bleeding. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed active bleeding from one of the two hypervascular lesions in segment IV. After angiographic embolization and conservative management, bleeding resolved. In April 2016, follow-up CT showed persistent hypervascular lesions without typical features of hepatocellular carcinoma. Additional MRI demonstrated hypervascular lesions with central necrosis. Because of suspicion for an atypical hepatocellular carcinoma, an elective surgical resection was planned.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of burning sensation and discomfort in her left breast without fever or systemic symptoms. A 36-year-old Asian man presented with a 4-month history of worsening headaches and complete right homonymous hemianopia. Two years earlier, he had a left occipital intracerebral hematoma of unknown cause. On examination, vital signs were normal, and neurologic testing confirmed the visual field defect without other focal deficits.

Noncontrast head CT showed a left occipital intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI revealed a left tentorial extra-axial enhancing mass with adjacent parenchymal hemorrhage, suggesting a cavernous angioma. The patient underwent a left occipital craniotomy; intraoperatively, the mass was found to invade the falx cerebri and adjacent cortex, limiting resection to subtotal removal. Postoperative CT showed no complications.

Histopathological examination demonstrated spindle cells forming masses with branching ectatic vasculature, focal collagenous regions, and up to 20 mitoses per ten high-power fields. Immunohistochemical studies showed strong immunoreactivity for CD31, CD99, and Fli-1, with scattered S100-positive cells, and negative staining for CD34, EMA, desmin, muscle-specific actin, and Bcl-2.

He reported one month of poor appetite, weight loss, and subjective fevers, and several days of diarrhea without abdominal pain, vomiting, cough, or dyspnea. On examination, he was febrile (39.4 °C), hypotensive (91/60 mmHg, improved with IV fluids), tachycardic (130 bpm), and lethargic. Initial labs showed leukocytosis (31 151/µL) and hyponatremia (Na 121 mEq/L). A chest radiograph was clear. Abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and enlarged peripancreatic lymph nodes. He was admitted to the ICU with presumed sepsis and started on vancomycin, piperacillin–tazobactam, and metronidazole. He then developed acute hypoxic respiratory failure and septic shock requiring intubation; post‐intubation chest radiograph showed new bilateral infiltrates. Blood cultures remained negative. Lumbar puncture demonstrated an opening pressure of 35 cm H₂O, 1825 RBCs/dL, 1 WBC/dL, glucose 65 mg/dL, and protein 36 mg/dL, and acyclovir was started empirically. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for bacterial, viral, fungal, and Pneumocystis jirovecii cultures. Initial sputum smears for acid‐fast bacilli were negative.

clinical_record:
A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presented with bilateral breast lumps of one-week duration. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and had previously regular menstrual cycles. On examination, the left breast had a 4 × 4 cm hard lump in the lower inner quadrant fixed to the chest wall; the right breast had a firm, mobile 1 × 1 cm lump in the lower outer quadrant. MRI showed a 3.8 × 3.5 cm irregular spiculated mass in the left breast suspicious for malignancy and a 2.3 × 1.5 cm well-defined lesion in the right breast with a type 1 contrast enhancement pattern (< 6% probability of malignancy) and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound and bone scan were negative for metastases. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the left breast lump revealed poorly cohesive clusters of ductal cells with pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and prominent nucleoli; myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei were absent. FNAC of the left axillary lymph node showed similar malignant cells. FNAC of the right breast lump showed three-dimensional clusters of hyperchromatic cells with prominent nucleoli and scattered pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures admixed with benign ductal cells and myoepithelial cells; a few bare nuclei were seen. Cytologic diagnosis was duct cell carcinoma of both breasts with left axillary lymph node metastasis. A core-needle biopsy of the left breast confirmed infiltrative duct cell carcinoma that was estrogen- and progesterone-receptor positive. On the basis of the physical examination results, the right breast lump was suspected to be a fibroadenoma. Hence, lumpectomy was performed.

clinical_record:
A 48-year-old otherwise healthy woman presented with a 5-day history of headache, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination and laboratory tests were within normal limits. She was diagnosed with tension headache and sinusitis and discharged on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. Three days later, her headache had resolved but vomiting persisted twice daily; she was treated with an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor for suspected gastroesophageal reflux. Over the following week, she developed ataxia, diplopia, and recurrence of her headache. 

She presented to the emergency department, and a T2-weighted MRI of the head showed increased signaling of the left temporal lobe, bilateral pontine regions, left peridentate nucleus, and cervical spinal cord. These findings were thought to represent an acute demyelinating process. Clinical suspicion for myasthenia gravis was high, and she was administered a trial of pyridostigmine without improvement. During hospitalization, her blood pressure rose to 190/90 mmHg, serum sodium was 123 mEq/L, glucose 176 mg/dL, and white-cell count 12,800 cells/mL. Neurologically, she had decreased sensorium, hallucinations, diminished attention span, and gait disturbance. A lumbar puncture showed an elevated opening pressure. 

Based on radiographic, laboratory, and clinical findings, a diagnosis of acute demyelinating encephalopathy was made, and suspicions of infectious encephalitis, collagen vascular disease, and toxic encephalitis were high. She received plasmapheresis without improvement. A follow-up T2-weighted MRI showed progressive enlargement of the bilateral pontine regions with hydrocephalus and mass effect on the fourth ventricle. Because of the absence of pathological enhancement of the pons, this was felt to represent either an aggressive demyelinating process or a low-grade glioma. The patient continued to deteriorate, became comatose, and died approximately four weeks after admission.

clinical_record:
A 60-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of epigastric abdominal pain, unintentional 33 lb weight loss, and intermittent melena. Her medical history was notable for irritable bowel syndrome and diet-controlled gluten intolerance; she denied tobacco and alcohol use. On examination, her abdomen was soft and nontender without organomegaly. Laboratory testing showed normocytic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 11.6 g/dL. An abdominal CT scan was unremarkable. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a 1.5 cm semipedunculated polyp (Paris Isp) in the gastric body, the same color as the surrounding mucosa, with a smooth surface lacking overlying mucus or prominent vessels. There was a heterogeneous surface pattern with uniform pitting near the base; no ulcerations or depressions were noted. The polyp was completely resected by snare polypectomy, and several other small sessile polyps were biopsied.
