A 53-year-old Hispanic man with no prior comorbidities presented with a two-week history of recurrent cough, nonmassive hemoptysis, and central chest pain. One month earlier, he had mild COVID-19 not requiring hospitalization. He also reported fatigue, myalgias, and anorexia but denied fever, dyspnea, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

On examination, he was tachycardic but in no acute distress; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (25.56×10^3/μL), blood urea nitrogen 107 mg/dL, creatinine 5.8 mg/dL (baseline unknown), mild transaminitis, hyponatremia, and hypoalbuminemia. Urinalysis and urine indices were ordered.

A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral scattered infiltrates with a denser consolidation in the right upper lobe. Noncontrast chest CT revealed multiple peripheral patchy consolidations in both lungs, some cavitating. These findings were interpreted as multifocal pneumonia.

He received intravenous azithromycin and ceftriaxone, intravenous bicarbonate, and emergent hemodialysis for acute kidney injury. Blood, sputum, and urine cultures were obtained, and PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 was negative.

A 54-year-old African American woman with poorly controlled hypertension, a 15 pack-year smoking history, and alpha-thalassemia anemia presented after 3 weeks of progressive blurred vision, fatigue, headache, and orthopnea. She was referred for hypertensive retinopathy evaluation, where her blood pressure measured 220/130 mmHg and she had cotton-wool spots on funduscopic exam. In the emergency department, her systolic pressure reached 230 mmHg. On examination, jugular venous pressure was 14 cm above the sternal angle; heart sounds were distant without pulsus paradoxus; lungs were clear; and there was no peripheral edema. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL (baseline 10 g/dL), creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 11 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 110 mm/hr. Chest radiography demonstrated a markedly enlarged cardiac silhouette with mild pulmonary congestion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large circumferential pericardial effusion (2.24 cm) with early right ventricular diastolic collapse, respirophasic mitral inflow variation, and a dilated inferior vena cava. A man in his 50s with a 12-year history of recurrent follicular lymphoma presented with a subacute, multifocal, pruritic, painful eruption that began on the abdomen and then involved the scalp, groin, and extremities. He denied fevers, chills, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. His medications included oxycodone, duvelisib (a PI3K inhibitor), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, all started 14 months earlier for lymphoma management. clinical_record:
A 70-year-old Japanese man presented with dysphagia and was diagnosed with T3N0M0 esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 6.6%), percutaneous coronary intervention, and radiotherapy for laryngeal cancer. He underwent two courses of 5-fluorouracil/docetaxel/cisplatin and then thoracoscopic esophagectomy with retrosternal gastric tube reconstruction and cervical esophagogastrostomy.

On postoperative day 4, cervical wound erythema with pus and saliva discharge appeared; drainage and intravenous tazobactam/piperacillin were initiated. Despite nutritional support and improved albumin levels, a refractory anastomotic fistula persisted, and Enterobacter cloacae was cultured from the wound. On day 60, salvage reconstruction with a free jejunal autograft and pectoralis major muscle flap coverage was performed.

Fifteen days after reconstruction, he developed worsening low back pain and fever (38.2 °C). Examination revealed lumbar spinal tenderness and bilateral leg weakness without sensory loss. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9200/µL and C-reactive protein of 9.86 mg/dL. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. clinical_record:
A 27-year-old man with a history of a 5 mm‐thick melanoma on his posterior neck treated six years earlier by wide local excision (no sentinel lymph node biopsy, no adjuvant therapy) presented with hemoptysis and dyspnea. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was notable only for scattered breath sounds without stridor. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 3.1 × 2.7 × 3.6 cm mass in the right lower lobe. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of the lung lesion demonstrated a malignant small round blue cell tumor. Molecular studies were negative for an EWSR1 translocation but otherwise were interpreted as consistent with Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET). 

Positron emission tomography (PET)/CT showed an FDG-avid right lower lobe mass and an intensely FDG-avid, partially calcified 4.1 × 2.3 × 2.8 cm expansile lesion within the right hyoid bone. Ultrasound–guided core needle biopsy of the hyoid lesion was nondiagnostic, yielding only rare atypical epithelial cells amidst lymphocytes.

A multidisciplinary sarcoma tumor board concluded that the hyoid lesion most likely represented a synchronous primary bone tumor (e.g., plasmacytoma, chondrosarcoma, or osteosarcoma). Given his pulmonary symptoms and the potential for chemotherapy to treat both lesions, he received 14 cycles of vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, and etoposide (VCD/IE). 

Mid-treatment PET/CT demonstrated a substantial decrease in size and complete metabolic response of the lung mass but development of right neck adenopathy and interval growth of the hyoid bone lesion, suggesting a distinct pathology.

reviewer_a.reason: The lung mass is identified as a malignant small round blue cell tumor, consistent with Ewing sarcoma/PNET, not a general lung cancer.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: lung mass
reviewer_b.reason: Lung cancer is a different entity; the case is about a possible metastasis or a new primary, not primary lung cancer.

clinical_record:
A 54-year-old woman with a history of stage III invasive ductal breast carcinoma treated with mastectomy and chemoradiation 4 years earlier presented with urinary frequency, worsening right-sided pelvic pain, and weight loss. MRI of the pelvis showed multiple fibroids and a heterogeneous 9.4 cm lesion involving the right uterine fundus/cornua. Intraoperatively, the mass was found in the right retroperitoneal space, tracking along the broad ligament and encasing the right external iliac artery; it was transected from the right uterine cornua. Grossly, the specimen was a detached, fragmented, ill-defined mass (14 × 12 × 4 cm) with fleshy solid and cystic components, central hemorrhage, and necrosis. A 32-year-old Han Chinese man, a professional driver, presented with a 4-year history of a slowly enlarging pigmented lesion on the upper left lip vermilion. He first noticed a 1 cm × 0.5 cm macule, which progressively increased in size without symptoms. After 3 years, he noted brownish discoloration of the skin above the vermilion. He had no significant medical or family history, and he did not smoke or drink.

On examination, multiple pigmented papules of various sizes involved the vermilion of the upper left lip, with brownish skin discoloration extending from 0.5 cm medial to the left angle of the mouth to the left philtral ridge. The lip was slightly swollen. Intraorally, a 1.5 cm lesion extended from the labial frenum to 0.5 cm medial to the left angle of the mouth; it was non-tender, non-indurated, and exhibited focal ulcerations. No cervical lymphadenopathy or other skin lesions were found.

Results of a complete blood count, biochemical profile, and urinalysis were within normal limits. Chest radiography was unremarkable. A computed tomography scan of the head and neck was performed to assess local extent of the lesion and to evaluate regional lymph nodes.

reviewer_b.reason: Laugier-Hunziker syndrome is a benign condition with multiple mucocutaneous macules, not a progressive enlarging lesion with ulceration; the clinical picture is malignant.

clinical_record:
A 50-year-old woman with hypertension and COPD first presented 5 months before admission with lower abdominal pain and decreased bowel movements; she was diagnosed with constipation. One month later, she returned with left lower-quadrant pain and low-grade fevers and was treated with ciprofloxacin and metronidazole for presumed diverticulitis. Symptoms partially improved, but she then had right upper-quadrant pain; abdominal CT was performed and incidentally revealed a confluent retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass encasing surrounding vessels. A HIDA scan confirmed cholecystitis, and she underwent cholecystectomy. 

One month after surgery, she had 5 days of progressively worsening, constant epigastric pain with nausea, vomiting, fatigue, anorexia, decreased urine output, and a 20-lb weight loss over 4 months. She denied fevers, chills, dysuria, or GI bleeding. On exam, blood pressure was 162/91 mmHg, pulse 79, and she had slight epigastric tenderness without guarding. Labs showed sodium 146 mEq/L, potassium 5.1 mEq/L, creatinine 8.18 mg/dL (baseline 0.8), WBC 10.4 K/uL, hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, and platelets 383 K/uL. Renal ultrasound demonstrated mild bilateral hydronephrosis, and postrenal obstruction was suspected. 

The following morning, a retrograde pyelogram showed bilateral hydronephrosis with extrinsic compression and medial deviation of the ureters, most prominently on the right. Ureteral stents were placed, relieving her obstruction, and her renal function subsequently returned to baseline.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.reason: While a retroperitoneal mass is present, there is no evidence in the record to suggest lymphoma. The mass is described as 'soft-tissue' and causing 'extrinsic compression' of ureters, which is more consistent with fibrosis than lymphoma without further biopsy or imaging characteristics.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: confluent retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass encasing surrounding vessels
reviewer_b.reason: Lymphoma is a possible differential for a retroperitoneal mass, but the clinical picture of extrinsic ureteral compression and medial deviation is classic for retroperitoneal fibrosis; no lymphadenopathy or other lymphoma features are described.

clinical_record:
A 28-year-old Hispanic man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis presented with a 10-day history of a pruritic eruption that began on the trunk and gradually spread to all extremities. He denied contact allergens, fever, or hyperhidrosis and had no prior history of atopic dermatitis, dermatophytosis, or hand eczema. On examination, he had scleral icterus and multiple dusky, thin plaques with a central collarette of scale on the face, neck, axillae, trunk, and extremities. On both hands and feet, there were hyperkeratotic plaques and deeply seated vesicles with a greenish-black hue, especially accentuated along the dermatoglyphic ridges. Laboratory testing showed total bilirubin 28.9 mg/dL (reference <1.2), direct bilirubin 17.7 mg/dL (<0.3), AST 78 IU/L, ALT 42 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 231 IU/L. A punch biopsy of the right palm revealed psoriasiform epidermal acanthosis, intraepidermal spongiosis, hyperkeratosis with sparse perivascular lymphocytic inflammation, and a dilated eccrine duct containing amorphous pink material. Gram, periodic acid–Schiff, and iron stains were negative. Punch biopsies of the chest and thigh were consistent with pityriasis rosea.

A 10-day-old, 40-kg male Chianina calf was referred for evaluation of progressive dyspnea, lethargy, and recumbency. On presentation, temperature was 38.5 °C; heart rate, 170 beats/min with regular rhythm; respiratory rate, 60 breaths/min; jugular pulses were present and mucous membranes were cyanotic, especially after brief exertion. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade IV/VI right apical systolic murmur and a more pronounced heartbeat on the right precordium. Lung sounds were harsh bronchovesicular. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia at 170 beats/min. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe dilation of the right atrium and right ventricle, a markedly hypoplastic left ventricle with a severely reduced mitral valve orifice, a 16 mm interatrial defect in the upper septum, and a 6 mm muscular interventricular defect in the dorsal septum. An oblique parasternal long-axis view revealed two great vessels arising in parallel from the right ventricle, differentiated by coronary arteries from one vessel and by left and right pulmonary arteries from the other. Color-flow Doppler showed severe tricuspid regurgitation and bidirectional shunting at both septal defects. Agitated saline contrast injected via the left jugular vein produced bubbles in the left atrium and ventricle and exiting the right ventricle through both great vessels.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.decisive_span: markedly hypoplastic left ventricle with a severely reduced mitral valve orifice
reviewer_a.reason: The record describes a hypoplastic left ventricle, which is a component of HLHS, but the primary diagnosis is the double-outlet right ventricle, which is a distinct and more specific finding.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: two great vessels arising in parallel from the right ventricle
reviewer_b.missing_or_conflicting_component: HLHS typically has aortic atresia and a single ventricle; here both great vessels arise from the right ventricle.
reviewer_b.reason: The presence of two well-formed great arteries from the right ventricle is not consistent with HLHS.

A 48-year-old man with a 12-year history of perianal fistula presented with recent mucinous discharge, pain, and perianal induration. One year earlier, he had undergone incision and drainage of a recurrent perianal abscess. 

On examination, there were two indurated, ulcerative lesions each 7 cm in diameter and three external fistula openings around the anus; there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Upper endoscopy was unremarkable. Colonoscopy showed the internal fistula opening at the right side of the dentate line, with otherwise normal mucosa in the rectum and colon on digital and endoscopic examination.

Abdominopelvic CT and MRI demonstrated a well-defined mass at the level of the anorectal junction extending into the right ischiorectal fossa, with enlarged pelvic lymph nodes but no inguinal nodal or distant metastases.

Histological examination of a biopsy specimen from the indurated area revealed mucinous adenocarcinoma. A serum carcinoembryonic antigen level was within the normal range.

A 30-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman was referred at 32 weeks’ gestation after an abnormal routine ultrasound. She had no significant medical history, no medication use, and no history of trauma. Previous prenatal care had been irregular.  
Transabdominal ultrasound showed bilateral ventriculomegaly with dilation of both frontal and occipital horns, irregular ventricular walls, multiple hyperechoic regions with indistinct margins within the ventricular lumens, and a roughened-appearing choroid plexus.  
Fetal Doppler ultrasound demonstrated normal middle cerebral artery perfusion.  
Fetal MRI confirmed bilateral ventricular enlargement and identified areas of high signal intensity on T1-weighted images and low signal intensity on T2-weighted images within the ventricles.  
A comprehensive workup—including a TORCH panel, platelet count, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, plasminogen levels, von Willebrand factor, factor V Leiden, protein S, protein C, and antiplatelet antibodies—returned within normal limits.

reviewer_a.reason: The record explicitly states 'bilateral ventriculomegaly' in a fetal context, directly matching the candidate.

reviewer_b.decisive_span: bilateral ventriculomegaly
reviewer_b.reason: Fetal ventriculomegaly is a descriptive finding, not the specific hemorrhagic etiology.
